tip: brukar plus an infinitive means usually or tend to: Jag brukar klaga = I usually complain.
Laugh at something is skratta åt, not på or till: skrattar åt skämtet = laughs at the joke.
Swedish has no separate continuous form. springer means both I run and I am running.
For things resting flat Swedish uses ligger, not är: Boken ligger i lådan = the book is in the box.
Start a sentence with an adverb like Faktiskt and the verb comes before the subject: Faktiskt tycker jag.
inte ens means not even, and sits between har and försökt: har inte ens försökt.
man is a generic you or one, for people in general: ser man = you see, one sees.
kunde is the past of kan (can): kunde inte hitta = couldn't find.
Superlatives take den plus the -aste form plus a definite noun: den kallaste månaden.
brukade is the past of brukar and means used to: brukade inte gilla = didn't use to like.
Commands use the plain verb form with no pronoun: Sväng = turn.
samma is followed by a plain noun with no definite ending: samma stad, not samma staden.
hoppas always ends in -s even though it is active: Jag hoppas = I hope.
Yes or no questions start with the verb: Ska vi ses...? = Shall we meet...?
hem is home as a direction you move toward; hemma is home as a location: kommer hem = come home.
Adjectives add -t with ett-words: ett stort hus. On its own it would be stor.
Comparatives add -are and use än for than: smutsigare än igår = dirtier than yesterday.
For an equal comparison use lika plus adjective plus som: lika bra som = just as good as.
sina means their own and points back to the subject of the clause: sina grannar = their own neighbors.
Longer adjectives form the comparative with mer, not -are: mer intressant = more interesting.
kommer att plus an infinitive is the future will: kommer att snöa = will snow.
The -s ending makes a passive here: ses = is seen or takes place, from se (to see).
